canberra.title: I haven’t stopped thinking about ‘You Can See Everything’ since I left the cinema
canberra.snippet: I have thought about Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s new documentary almost every second since I’ve walked out of the ci...
canberra.content:
Disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes is back in the news with the release of the documentary ‘You Can See Everything’. Photo: A24.

I have thought about Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s new documentary almost every second since I’ve walked out of the cinema.

The near three-hour documentary places Fielder in the home of disgraced Theranos founder and convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes and her husband, Billy Evans, 34 days before she is sent to a Texas prison for defrauding investors out of $700-900 million for her blood testing machine, which didn’t work.

Holmes and her husband maintain her innocence, claiming the machine can do everything she said it could. However, the film is less about proving guilt or innocence and instead asks: Is Holmes the greatest conwoman of all time, or just the face of other people’s manipulation?

The film can be split into two parts. The first is the 34 days leading to her being sent to prison.

We see how she operates day to day; we dig into how she sees the world, and most importantly, how she and her husband interact with each other and the rest of the world.

From the moment the film starts, it’s clear Nathan doesn’t trust Elizabeth and Billy. He’s not afraid to call out their weird behaviour and comments that don’t line up.

Nathan and Billy, in particular, clash over what Billy lets Elizabeth say and do, from taking a bowl of eggs from her because she isn’t beating them correctly to jumping in when pressed about her relationship with her former business partner.

While Elizabeth’s love for Billy is never questioned, it does ask: Is Billy involved with Elizabeth out of love or opportunity?

The first half’s most interesting moments, however, come when it focuses on how Elizabeth takes in information and communicates it to others.

Two scenes in particular stand out: one where she is pressed about her sales pitch to investors and another where she’s asked to describe the famous Who’s on First joke.

These moments affect Fielder and lead him to develop a strange attraction to Elizabeth and the way her brain works, suggesting that Nathan may have fallen for Elizabeth’s manipulative nature, just as her staff and investors did.

The first half of the film ends with Elizabeth being escorted to prison, then it jumps two years from 2023 to 2025.

I’m going to be tight-lipped about this half of the film because the reveals here are bonkers. Most of the second half is spent with Billy, and a lot of it focuses on the decisions he makes for his wife now that she’s in prison.

It also highlights the unique ways they tell Elizabeth’s story, despite Nathan and Lance not being able to film or record her in prison.

The way they go about this is incredible, including the introduction of a famous actress with links to Elizabeth.

What Nathan and this actress discover is insane, and it fuels the idea that maybe Elizabeth has been manipulated this whole time.

From a technical viewpoint, this doco is unlike anything I’ve ever seen. It is purposely shot in a 4:3 or letterbox aspect ratio, meaning the sides of the screen are cut off.

This is an intentional stylistic choice that puts everything on screen in focus. There’s no background, there are rarely two people in the shot, and there’s often only one light source. It plays into the idea: do you really see everything like the title of the film suggests?

The score by Ari Balouzian is also rooted in mystery and uneasiness. It makes it difficult to form a clear opinion and instead leaves you feeling haunted by what you’ve learnt.

Unfortunately, no words I write can do this film justice. You Can See Everything is unlike anything else I’ve ever seen.

Instead of learning more about Elizabeth Holmes, I have more questions and, tragically, I, as well as everyone else who has seen this film, will never get them. That’s the beauty of this documentary.

Even with everything laid out in front of me, I still have no clue whether Elizabeth Holmes is a victim or the world’s greatest conwoman.

You Can See Everything is showing in cinemas across the country.

canberra.title: After 65 days away from home, a Canberra Hospital camera brings mum closer to her baby
canberra.snippet: For more than two months, Goulburn mother Erin Thorpe had barely seen life outside Canberra Hospital. Her newborn daughter, Aubree, was r...
canberra.content:
Goulburn mother Erin Thorpe can now watch her premature daughter, Aubree, via a live-streaming camera at Canberra Hospital. Photo: Naziya Alvi Rahman.

For more than two months, Goulburn mother Erin Thorpe had barely seen life outside Canberra Hospital.

Her newborn daughter, Aubree, was receiving specialist care, her five other children were at home, and even a quick trip to the shops left her anxious to return to her baby’s bedside.

Then a small camera at her baby’s cot, installed last week, changed everything.

For the first time in more than 65 days, Erin travelled home to surprise her children and attend her little boy’s kindergarten orientation. Aubree was still in hospital, but Erin could now see her daughter on her phone whenever she needed reassurance.

“I just log onto the phone, and I see her, and it’s fine,” she said.

Erin is among the first parents to benefit from AngelEye, a new live-streaming camera system introduced across all 39 beds in Canberra Hospital’s Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) and Special Care Nursery.

The technology allows parents to securely watch their premature or critically ill babies when they cannot be physically present, whether they are working, caring for other children or living interstate.

For Erin, whose sixth child was born at just 30 weeks and five days, the separation has been particularly difficult.

She spent four weeks in the hospital’s antenatal ward before Aubree was born and has since been staying at Ronald McDonald House to remain close to her daughter.

Her other five children have visited their baby sister only a handful of times.

“With children come germs, and I don’t really want them around her too much,” Erin said.

Now, they can watch Aubree from home through a secure video link shared by their father.

Senior neonatologist Dr Hazel Carlisle, who was the clinical lead on the AngelEye project, said some babies born extremely prematurely could spend three to six months in hospital.

Around 850 babies are admitted to Canberra Hospital’s NICU and Special Care Nursery each year. For families travelling from regional NSW, those lengthy stays can mean juggling work, other children and long periods away from home.

Dr Carlisle said parents had always been encouraged to spend as much time as possible at their baby’s bedside, but until now, they could not see their child once they left the hospital.

“There’s no substitute for parents being present, so it’s an added extra to assist with the care,” she said.

The cameras provide video only, without sound, and can operate in low light to avoid disturbing babies.

They also allow grandparents, siblings and other family members, including those overseas, to see a newborn they might otherwise be unable to visit.

The project was developed over several years following feedback from families through the hospital’s family-centred care committee.

Privacy has been another important consideration. Digital Canberra executive branch manager Monica Reeson said parents receive unique, secure logins, preventing them from accessing another baby’s feed.

Participation is voluntary, and cameras are switched off during medical procedures or whenever a family chooses not to use the service.

The system is not used for clinical monitoring. The $117,600 installation was funded by the Newborn Intensive Care Foundation, which has supported neonatal care at Canberra Hospital for more than 30 years.

Foundation chief executive officer Peter Cursley said the organisation had raised more than $1 million over that period to provide equipment and additional support for premature and critically ill babies.

Health Minister Marisa Paterson said the cameras would give families greater flexibility during an emotionally demanding time.

“While nothing can replace being at your baby’s bedside, the live streaming cameras provide reassurance and connection when families cannot be physically at hospital,” she said.

For Erin, that reassurance has already made a difference.

Aubree still needs time to overcome feeding difficulties before she can leave hospital, but her mother is beginning to imagine life beyond the neonatal unit.

“I’m hoping I’m through the thick of it, and I’m starting to see the light,” she said.

canberra.title: Parents can’t put the brakes on e-bikes, the nanny state must (and fast)
canberra.snippet: In Engadine, a 13-year-old e-bike rider tore through the monkey bar area of a local playground, striking a 5-year-old boy and breaking hi...
canberra.content:
Sure they’re fun, but they can be deadly. Photo: Taras Grebinets.

In Engadine, a 13-year-old e-bike rider tore through the monkey bar area of a local playground, striking a 5-year-old boy and breaking his leg.

In Albion Park, two kids on an e-bike collided with a car. The 11-year-old passenger was airlifted to Sydney Children’s Hospital, Randwick, with serious injuries, while the older child – 13 years old – was taken to Wollongong Hospital.

Meanwhile, in Lake Macquarie, a 14-year-old was treated by paramedics before being taken to hospital after crashing their e-bike into a stationary car.

Three frightening incidents with serious consequences for the children and families involved. All within a few weeks. The last two incidents, within 20 minutes of each other.

Canberra has seen its share of e-bike mayhem this year, with sports fields, golf courses and South.Point Shopping Centre bearing the scars.

It’s not surprising trauma doctors are raising concerns about the number of children ending up in hospital as a result of e-bike or e-scooter accidents. With Christmas around the corner, and the potential for more e-bikes and young riders on the roads, the issue is pressing.

Recent statistics from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) show the rate of hospitalisations for “the transport group that includes e-bikes” has more than tripled in nine years, while hospitalisations for the category including e-scooters have tripled in five years.

Hospitalisation rates among 12- to 15-year-olds have surged in both categories.

Importantly, the report can’t give specific counts on e-scooter or e-bike injuries because “hospital data place these devices within broader transport categories”. Basically, your average battery-powered teenager has been lumped in with Granny’s mobility aid. New national hospital codes have since been introduced to address this.

That said, anecdotal evidence and common sense lead us towards certain conclusions. Clearly, the issue needs attention.

Speaking of common sense, why have we given children free rein over motorised vehicles?

With no minimum age, mandatory training or licensing system, we send them into the streets unsupervised and wonder why they (#notallteens) form little mobs and take their personal vehicles where they’re not meant to go, skidding through shopping centres, tearing up playing fields and intimidating non-motorised adults.

Children can’t handle Lego without ending up with a brick up their nose. For a while, kids everywhere were exploding gelatinous toys in the microwave because TikTok told them to.

Children misuse things, get overexcited and make poor choices. And that’s okay, because they are children. They’ve not yet developed their frontal lobe.

What’s our excuse?

A mid-range e-bike comes with a price tag around $2000. That’s a lot of pocket money.

Clearly, the appeal of these things isn’t limited to children. Deeper, grown-up pockets are required to acquire one.

Even my husband- mid-40s- while on holiday in Wollongong, forlornly floated the idea of getting an e-bike as he watched a group of cool kids zoom past (despite the fact we live nowhere near a single footpath).

And I get it. From the environmental scourge of loom bands to squishies filled with skin-bubbling solvents and Elf on the bloody Shelf, I’m often a victim of the call of but Mum, everybody has one!

In many suburbs, an e-bike has somehow become the quintessential accessory of a modern childhood.

Which brings me to the government’s doorstep.

Under current NSW Road Rules, a child of any age can ride an e-bike and carry a passenger.

While there have been rumblings of introducing a minimum age limit, the issue has been delayed – potentially until after the state election – as the state government prioritises the targeting of illegal and modified e-bikes.

Meanwhile, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) is seeking public feedback on proposed national e-bike safety standards.

Just quietly, the only mods we made to pedal-powered bikes involved a water bottle in the spokes or tassels on the handlebars. No harm, no foul.

Curiously, privately owned e-scooters are already illegal to ride on NSW public roads and paths.

Whether it’s a blanket ban, introducing age limits, or a licensing system to curb the freedom of anonymity, we clearly need to introduce some boundaries.

But why do we need government intervention to do it?

The same reason many parents welcomed social media laws. Or the banning of “squishies” at school. Because it’s bloody difficult to fight off the never-ending barrage of new technology and fast-burning trends constantly coming for our kids with more virality than gastro through a daycare centre.

And there’s a world of difference between telling your child you’ve decided they’re the only kid on the street who can’t have a TikTok, laser pointer or e-bike, and telling them it’s illegal.

It might be a cop out, but sometimes we need the government to be the fun police.

Sidebar: Would anyone like to sign my petition to ban Elf on the Shelf?

canberra.title: Aranya Acres is stirring up a melting pot of cuisines, culture and community
canberra.snippet: It’s peaceful here. So peaceful, I swear I can hear Jovi’s busy mind whirring as he reveals his grand plans for this stunning vineyard, c...
canberra.content:
From artisanal sourdough to backyard beekeepers, Jovi says he opts for hyper-local sources where he can. Photo: Supplied.

It’s peaceful here.

So peaceful, I swear I can hear Jovi’s busy mind whirring as he reveals his grand plans for this stunning vineyard, currently in the midst of a major metamorphosis.

A group of diners makes to leave and Jovi jumps up for farewells.

One of them gushes about the meal and hospitality, sharing her excitement about hosting her local yoga group at this vibrant venue.

It’s a small moment that neatly captures what Jovi Arya and partner Emily Cunich are creating at Aranya Acres, a place where good food, culture and community come together.

It’s been eight months since the couple took over the restaurant where they once worked, and Jovi says it’s involved some trial and error.

Previously operating as Contentious Character, the property has been split three ways to incorporate Aranya Acres restaurant and Sapling Yard Wines Cellar Door and Winery, while the Wamboin Hills Estate tends the vineyards.

The idea behind Aranya Acres is to create a welcoming atmosphere where locals and visitors can come together to enjoy the fruits of our region.

“The food, the presentation and the service are still top tier – we don’t want to compromise on that – but we want people to feel comfortable.”

Originally from Sydney, Jovi Arya lived in Canberra for nine years, honing his hospitality skills in venues like Akiba, Lazy Su and Bar Beirut, before deciding to move to Bungendore in 2021, where he now lives with partner Emily, eight-week-old baby Niya, his parents and two dogs.

“I love Bungendore and this area because everyone is extremely friendly and community-minded,” he says. “Everyone really gets along and helps each other out.”

While he once worked the floor at Contentious Character, Jovi never imagined he’d end up owning the restaurant.

“I’ve always done front-of-house, so getting my head around food costs, salaries, tax and all that stuff has taken some time,” he says.

Jovi is quick to credit his behind-the-scenes team, including his partner, Emily.

With an Art History and Curatorship degree, Emily leads the charge in culture, events and marketing, from sculpture gardens and burlesque performances to hands-on craft workshops where she mixes cocktails with crochet, felting or embroidery classes.

Meanwhile, chef de cuisine Praneel Singh conjures “wizardry” in the kitchen.

Previously head chef at Capitol Bar and Grill, Praneel and Jovi first met at Lake George Winery.

Over the next six years, they dreamed of their own winery.

“We always had it in our minds and had a business plan ready to go, but Contentious Character didn’t occur to me because I didn’t think it could be split the way it has been.”

The restaurant takes a multicultural approach to contemporary Australian food, with creative menus which bring together a diverse range of cuisines and traditions rather than relying on typical “modern Australian” regulars.

Aranya’s summer menu is inspired by Goan, Portuguese and Mediterranean cuisines, pulling in Australian native flavours. Photo: Supplied.

Menus change seasonally but remain impressively inclusive, with substantial vegan, vegetarian and pescetarian options, and most are celiac-friendly.

Accessibility is a recurring theme at Aranya – whether that be dietary restrictions, budgets, or simply making themselves easier to reach.

The team is currently developing a monthly Heritage menu, offering both high-end dining and traditional street food options.

“Once a month we’ll host, for example, a Japanese night, and the Heritage Series will be a five-course Japanese-style degustation, while the Heritage Street option will be something a bit more accessible and casual, like a ramen and hip hop night.”

The Local’s Lunch Special offers seafood, pasta and wine, and set menus at affordable prices, while – in a huge coup for the area – Jovi has recently partnered with Uber Eats.

“I’m just trying to show them there is demand and that people in the area will become drivers,” he says.

“I think there’ll be a huge uptake and it will eventually support all Bungendore businesses.”

From its progressive menu of quality cuisine and showcase of locally produced wine, to its open invitation to community groups, artists and musicians, Aranya Acres is cultivating a sophisticated bohemian vibe.

“I like the intersectionality of bringing people from all walks of life.”

Right now, Jovi is focused on planning for Bungendore High School’s inaugural formal event, as well as regular events like Thursday night trivia and live music every Friday.

Always thinking ahead, Jovi has his sights set on larger-scale outdoor events, with a view to get everyone safely “home by 10 pm”.

“I can host up to 300 people for things like special whiskey and beer events, or comedy festivals. I want to do daytime events like silent discos,” he says.

“We’ll work to organise chartered buses, so people are coming safely and leaving safely.

For locals, Aranya Acres offers a cosy home away from home. For visitors, it’s a destination worth travelling for – and offering plenty of reasons to return.

Aranya Acres is located at 810 Norton Rd, Wamboin. It’s open from 11 am to 3 pm and from 5 pm to 9 pm, Thursday to Sunday (it’s closed Monday to Wednesday).

canberra.title: Striking oil: Mazda bets big in diesel. Are they right?
canberra.snippet: It wasn’t so long ago that it looked like diesel might just save the internal combustion engine. For a long time, diesel engines were for...
canberra.content:
Despite most brands moving away from diesels for anything except 4x4s, Mazda still offers an innovative six-cylinder oiler in the CX-60. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

It wasn’t so long ago that it looked like diesel might just save the internal combustion engine.

For a long time, diesel engines were for trucks, trains and tractors. Noisy and agricultural, they had their place – and it wasn’t in cars.

That was until small, ultra-efficient turbo-diesels became readily available in passenger cars, particularly European ones. From the 1990s through to the 2010s, they became more refined, more efficient and cleverer.

Then, Dieselgate happened, and while I won’t delve into the whole history here, it’s safe to say it looked like it would put the nail in the coffin for diesel passenger cars when it turned out they weren’t so clean after all.

While diesel has mostly disappeared from passenger cars, it’s still the go-to fuel for the dual-cab utes Aussies buy more than anything else. But these aren’t immune from issues, as features designed to actually make them cleaner – such as diesel particulate filters – have only made some more unreliable.

Mazda mustn’t have got the memo, though. Despite the shift away from diesel in most market segments, Mazda decided to build an entirely new diesel engine a few years ago. And it’s magnificent.

This impressive 3.3-litre inline-six turbo-diesel reminds us why diesel managed to take off in the first place.

But with diesel prices bordering on highway robbery, does it still make sense?

The six-cylinder petrol and diesel versions of the CX-60 are identically priced for 2026, compounding the potential savings from better fuel economy. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

What is it?

Dubbed the ‘D50e’ in Mazda-speak, this engine is only available in the brand’s Large Architecture models.

The one we’re testing here is the smallest of the lot, the CX-60 in middling GT specification. Priced at $65,640 before on-road costs, identical to the equivalent petrol version, consider this car Mazda’s attempt at creating a BMW X3.

Combining a straight-six engine, a rear-biased AWD system (standard on all six-cylinder and plug-in hybrid versions), and a genuinely plush interior, it delivers a cut-price luxury SUV experience.

These Large Architecture models were created as part of a push from Mazda to head further upmarket – a push which hasn’t exactly paid off in terms of sales figures. Still, the CX-60 is unequivocally good-looking and well-equipped.

This GT version may only be in the middle of the range, but it features 20-inch black alloy wheels, a panoramic sunroof, heated seats, a heated steering wheel, leather upholstery with contrast stitching, wireless Apple CarPlay, a head-up display, and driver assistance tech that is more innovative than most cars these days.

As for the diesel engine powering this one, it’s far more innovative than the clattery thing you’d find on a farm. Designed to be powerful yet economical, Mazda’s aims certainly seem to have been achieved.

With outputs of 187 kW and 550 Nm, it certainly has performance duly covered. Considering those numbers, along with its size and cylinder count, the fuel economy promise of a mere 5.0 litres per 100km sounds almost far-fetched.

That is, until you consider its 48-volt mild hybrid system that can intermittently shut the engine off for brief periods when cruising – although even then, that kind of economy from a six-cylinder engine still seems like it would only occur in a lab.

It’s safe to say what happened during my week with it surprised me.

The CX-60 features a nicely designed, well-trimmed interior regardless of which variant you choose, with this GT model representing a good midpoint in the range. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

What’s it like to live with?

Although I’ve driven many versions of the CX-60 and Mazda’s other Large Architecture models before, this was the first time I’ve driven this six-cylinder diesel.

It was clear immediately that this is the best version of the CX-60 I’ve driven yet.

The only visual way to tell this diesel apart from a six-pot petrol version is a little red “D” tag on one of the badges on the boot lid. However, there is an audible reminder, as there’s some diesel clatter to be heard externally on idle.

From inside the CX-60, though, the engine is very well muted. Whether at idle or when burying your foot on the loud pedal, it’s never all that loud. Even when it is, it doesn’t sound too diesel-ish either.

A big part of this engine’s appeal is how it delivers its power. The nature of turbo-diesel engines means their torque is accessible low down in the rev range – all of it is available from 1500-2400rpm in this instance – and pardon the overused analogy, but this thing really does pull like a freight train.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

There’s a tiny hint of turbo lag at first, but once it spools up, it absolutely legs it thanks to all that diesel torque. As a result, it’s not what you’d call a sporty engine, but in a straight line it’s undeniably pacey.

As someone prone to being liberal with the throttle inputs, you’d think that with six whole cylinders this engine would drink like a fish. Even more so when you consider the six-cylinder petrol version tends to use at least 9.0 litres per 100 km in my experience, never getting close to Mazda’s 7.4-litre claim.

But after 580 km of testing in a week, this CX-60 had only sipped diesel at 6.3 litres per 100 km. It even had just over one-quarter of a tank left.

Diesel might be on par with printer ink for how much of a pricing rort it is right now, but that kind of efficiency certainly softens the blow. My results were an increase over Mazda’s claim, but with more highway driving in the mix, I can see it dipping into the fives.

20-inch black alloy wheels are standard on this GT model. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

This little red D is the only indication that this is a diesel... aside from the sound at idle. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

This 3.3-litre diesel packs outputs of 187 kW and 550 Nm. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Mazda is understandably proud of offering a six-cylinder engine these days. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Part of this efficiency, I am sure, comes down to the mild hybrid system. Since diesel engines don’t require spark plugs to ignite the fuel and instead use compression, it seemed as though it could shut off and reactivate the engine far more often (and far more smoothly) than the equivalent petrol engine could.

Speaking of, this CX-60 also felt far smoother than most others I’ve driven, thanks to a series of incremental updates Mazda has made since its 2023 launch.

The ride quality feels less jittery than earlier versions. The eight-speed automatic transmission – which doesn’t use a torque converter like most of its kind – felt less juddery here as well.

I told you this was the best CX-60 I’ve driven yet. This one finally made this car make sense.

The verdict

When it comes to the diesel CX-60, there’s really only one thing you need to know that hasn’t been mentioned already.

Using average Canberra fuel prices from FuelRadar and Mazda’s own fuel consumption claims, the diesel will cost you $2.81 less to run every 100 km. That’s a saving of over $350 a year if you drive as much as the average Aussie.

So Mazda might just be right to keep sticking with diesel. This engine is excellent, a real engineering marvel that a six-cylinder can be this economical. It makes the CX-60 a better car.

It’s a shame most people won’t buy it.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.
