2026 Mazda CX-60 D50e GT

  • $65,640 before on-road costs
  • 3.3-litre inline six-cylinder turbo diesel, 48-volt mild hybrid system, 187 kW/550Nm
  • Eight-speed automatic, all-wheel drive
  • 5.0 litres per 100km, 58-litre fuel capacity
  • 2073kg kerb weight.

Thanks to Mazda Australia for providing this vehicle for testing. Region has no commercial arrangement with Mazda Australia.

australia.title: Potty-mouthed MPs ranked as Australian parliament sets new swearing record
australia.snippet: One serial sweary offender, Jacqui Lambie, says it wouldn’t be an Australian parliament ‘without a few swear words thrown in’ Want to get...
australia.content:
When Liberal MP Garth Hamilton stormed out of parliament in June, slamming his hands on his desk and calling out “fucking bullshit” the speaker of the house, Milton Dick, called it “a new low” in federal politics.

Dick may have been on to something.

New analysis from Guardian Australia has found profanity and foul language has risen significantly in Australia’s parliament over the past 20 years, with some of today’s most prominent politicians among the chief culprits for swearing.

Before the year is even out, 2026 is the worst year on record for the use of swear words and language deemed “unparliamentary”. That number has risen by 78% since 2006.

Analysis of Hansard debate and procedure records has found that per million words spoken in parliament this year, approximately 37 have been profane – ranging from milder (“bloody”, “damn” and “crap”) to language considered strong, or even extreme.

While entitled to “parle hard”, language deemed unparliamentary by the speaker or Senate president is required to be withdrawn, or else MPs face ejection from the chamber.

So why bother?

Beyond the impact of pushing against regulation and etiquette, there is something to be said for the currency that outbursts gain when clipped and shared online – recently demonstrated by Greens senator Peter Whish-Wilson, who called for the country to “wake the fuck up” to One Nation’s use of social media algorithms in June.

But despite the politicians reaching for profanities at a record rate, Dick – the Labor MP who has been speaker of the house since 2022 – said he felt the tone and tenor of debate in parliament has gotten better in his time in the chair.

“Debate is fierce and strong, and apart from a few incidents, it has improved,” he said.

“Maybe it hasn’t appeared so because of the volume [of swearing], but when you analyse the words used … there are outbreaks of course, but I believe in everyone showing respect.”

And to be fair, most of parliament’s most swear-y politicians are in the Senate, not the house.

An oral tradition

Described as “the great Australian adjective” in 1894 by The Bulletin magazine, “bloody” appears to have suffered no fall from grace in the subsequent years, serving as the most commonly used swear word in parliament. Along with “damn”, “crap” and “bugger”, mild curses constitute 92% of all recorded bad language, with more severe terms such as “prick”, “shit” and “piss” used more sparingly.

Excluded from this figure are rare cases of colourful and creative terms that have been called for withdrawal. Harnessing the speaker’s unilateral power to flag unacceptable language, terms such as “bin chickens – used by Julian Hill, the MP for Bruce, in 2022 to describe the opposition in the house – have been ruled as unparliamentary.

Swearing and swearing allegiance

Much of this potty-talk comes from the Senate, which since 2006 has seen a 177% increase in the use of bad language. Among active parliamentary participants (those who have spoken at least 100,000 words in this period), Bill Heffernan was the lead offender. Despite speaking just 141,000 words between 2006 and 2016, the former Liberal senator had an expletive use-rate of 877 per million words spoken, 43 times the rate of all other parliamentarians.

Jacqui Lambie is the second-most sweary politician, responsible for 6% of total swearing in parliament at a rate of 406 per million words spoken – more than 19 times the average. But, like most of the politicians on this list, Lambie’s swearing is overwhelmingly mild – mostly words like “crap” or “bloody”.

“I try really hard not to swear, especially in the Senate chamber. It upsets my mum, she doesn’t even like me saying ‘bloody’,” Lambie said when we came to her with the statistics.

“It’s important to be respectful. But I am a straight shooter and sometimes things are just crap – and it’s hard not to say so. I don’t think it would be an Australian parliament without a few swear words thrown in.”

Not all occurrences of swearing in parliamentary records are “own-use”, or rather, swearing with intent. Quotes, such as reading out abuse a politician has received, or a quote from a document, account for some of it.

However, when excluding these cases our analysis shows that own-use swearing in parliament has nearly tripled over the last 20 years, from 6.4 per million words in 2006-9, to 18.9 in 2022-5.

Broken down by party, One Nation are the worst offenders, swearing for the sake of it at 7.4 times the rate of Labor – perhaps unsurprising, given that the party leader, Pauline Hanson, ranks fourth among discursively active politicians for use of foul language.

Dick said he had strived to improve the tone of discussion in parliament, believing that greater diversity in politics and in the chamber – with more women, more First Nations MPs and people from multicultural backgrounds – had also changed dynamics of debate.

Asked about recent heated moments in parliament, he said he recalled only two major moments in the lower house in recent years Hamilton’s June storm-out and fellow Liberal MP Dan Tehan’s demand to “cut the crap” in August.

“I want to ensure among our people and our democracy, that we fight hard to disagree more civilly … But I’m a big believer in upholding traditions and standards. When things get a bit heated, I’ll take firm action,” Dick said.

Notes on the analysis

Politicians’ speeches from both Houses of Parliament were analysed for the years 2006 to 2026. For each speech, the number of swearwords were counted using the these categories:

  • Mild: bloody, damn, crap, bugger, bastard, bulldust, arse, mongrel, boofhead, bollocks

  • Strong: prick, shit, bullshit, piss, piss off, dickhead, arsehole, shithouse, wanker

  • Extreme: fucking, cunt, fuck, fuck off, fucker, fucked, motherfucker

To control for politicians’ tenure length and verbosity affecting swearing totals, swearing numbers were converted to a rate per million words by dividing the total swearwords by the total number of words spoken for that politician in that year, or for the total time period.

To separate swearing in a politician’s own voice from quotes, idioms and literal uses, an LLM was used to read the speech text surrounding each swearword and sort these into categories. A random sample of the results were manually checked, to achieve an agreement of 97% on whether a use was the speaker’s own. Therefore these figures are approximate.

australia.title: ‘I wouldn’t say top 20 in the world, but it’s the best in Adelaide’: a day in Ebenezer Place, one of the world’s coolest streets
australia.snippet: The quiet East End restaurant and retail strip has ranked No 19 in Time Out’s latest list, the highest in Australia. Regulars say it’s al...
australia.content:
There’s a now-iconic line from The Simpsons, which aired more than 30 years ago, where Principal Skinner is trying to track down Bart, who has skipped school.

He goes looking for him in places he assumes children might hang out, including a museum and a youth group, but finds them empty.

He pauses and considers: “Am I so out of touch? … No. It’s the children who are wrong.”

I find myself asking a similar question perched on Ebenezer Place in Adelaide, recently ranked the world’s 19th coolest street by Time Out magazine.

Sipping on a glass of Gamay at 4pm on a Saturday at French brasserie Hey Jupiter, I look down the street to assess the level of “coolness” that convinced a global magazine this is one of the 28 streets in the world most worth visiting.

Adelaide is no stranger to the dizzying highs of global magazine lists, placing in the top 10 of the Economist’s most liveable cities index for eight of the past 10 years, much to the bemusement of the higher-ranked Melbourne and Sydney. But this time it’s won out: the only other Australian entry on the Time Out list, Ward Avenue in Sydney’s Potts Point, is ranked No 24.

In coolness, Adelaide wins.

Hey Jupiter is softening me to this idea. The French brasserie, with its vibrant green facade, sits alongside a South African eatery, vintage clothing outlet, record store and a jeweller.

The tree-lined street is open to one-way traffic and cars circle looking for a prime parking spot. Yet despite this it’s clean, bright and well-manicured, much like the crowd of young fashionistas and well-dressed older couples soaking up the vibe and sipping everything from vibrant matcha to lethal-looking martinis.

Almost two decades ago, that would have been me.

While diligently avoiding my university lectures, I would waste days – and nights – at a clothing store owned by my two best mates, which opened here in the mid-2000s.

I certainly thought it was cool then.

Edgy fashion outlets attracted musical acts like Van She and Pnau, who would randomly arrive along the strip with drinks in hand from a nearby wine store, as music wafted out of the shopfronts.

With street parties and events sponsored by big tobacco, there was a time when this street was the wild west of Adelaide’s east end.

Twenty years later, Ebenezer Place has had a glow-up, got some new roommates and been officially recognised as cool.

Christopher Arblaster, co-founder of clothing store Shop Pond (formerly A Flat Shop), also runs the adjacent vintage store, Filter Store. While surprised by the nomination, he’ll happily take the hype.

  • Sign up for the fun stuff with our rundown of must-reads, pop culture and tips for the weekend, every Sunday morning

“I think it shows more about the people who use the street. We have lovely neighbours, some really great shops and there’s quite a lot of activity along here for a quieter strip,” he says.

“I wouldn’t say it’s the 19th coolest street in the world – but it is a nice place to be.”

Surprise shout-out

It’s not that Ebenezer Place doesn’t deserve the accolade – but what, exactly, are the criteria?

Time Out recommends that visitors to the street “keep the vibes high” at nearby drinking haunts Nola and East End Cellars, catch an indie film at Palace Nova, or dine at Michelin Guide-recognised restaurants Golden Boy and Africola.

It names Ebenezer Place as the destination but suggests you widen the net some 500m to visit other restaurants on the city’s edge. It also points readers towards Rundle Street for its indie boutiques and high-end fashion labels.

The City of Adelaide seems equal parts excited and caught off-guard about the shout-out, posting a gushing message to social media with a photo of the wrong East End strip – bustling Vardon Avenue, not Ebenezer Place.

As 21-year-old Nicolas Garcia-Bellido Rodriguez and his mate, 20-year-old Eamon Ziersch-O’Connor, enjoy an ice cream at Ovo Coffee and Gelato, they say the strip evokes another continent entirely.

“It feels like I’m in Europe sitting here, and parts of Rundle Street feel the same too,” Nicolas says.

“I think it’s the proximity – it’s right near the Exeter Hotel, which is great. It hosts a lot of events here, which I think contributes to the vibe.”

Ata Alrimawi, 22, says the strip is his go-to place to relax and grab a coffee.

“I wouldn’t say top 20 in the world, but it’s the best in Adelaide for sure,” he says.

The state MP and minister for Adelaide, Lucy Hood, says the global ranking speaks to the passion and dedication of local businesses that have transformed Ebenezer Place into “a thriving and must-visit destination”.

A subjective list will always attract clicks and is rarely without its controversies. As my Gamay reaches the end of its final pour and the afternoon slips into evening, the people-watching has provided hours of entertainment.

I would still argue that the judges must have had a pretty biblical night along this street to convince them it’s one of the 20 best in the world.

But Ebenezer Place has always had its charms. As the sun fades, I decide to embrace this new, if surprising chapter in the story of this understated 120-metre long strip. Maybe it’s me who’s out of touch, and the children were right all along.

australia.title: Victoria faced devastating bushfires and an ‘extinction emergency’ this year. So why is nature missing from the election?
australia.snippet: As Victorians head to the polls, experts accuse both major parties of deserting environmental policy Sign up for climate and environment ...
australia.content:
The election year in Victoria began with devastating bushfires and record-breaking heat. Vulnerable grey-headed flying foxes perished in their thousands in the worst mass mortality event for the species since 2019’s black summer. Fires, which burned through more land than Black Saturday, destroyed most of the remaining Victorian habitat for endangered pink cockatoos and eastern bristlebirds.

A “shocker” of a ski season followed – the combined effect of global heating and an historic El Niño – while deadly H5 bird flu arrived in the state’s south-west, wreaking havoc among coastal birds, seals and dolphins. A key population of Leadbeater’s possums, the state’s animal emblem, were evacuated from their home at Yellingbo conservation area and placed in a specially developed refuge after their numbers halved in a matter of months – thought to have been taken by predators.

Yet less than a week from polling day, nature has barely rated a mention in the campaign. So why has the environment been so absent?

“We’ve got every single political party basically deserting the environment space,” says Prof David Lindenmayer, a conservation biologist at the Australian National University. “I can’t speak lowly enough about the quality of the environmental policies of the parties. It’s hard to believe how badly it’s unravelled in the last 12 years in Victoria.”

Labor’s track record is “woeful”, he says, while accusing the Coalition of plans to bring back native forest logging under the guise of bushfire management.

A report released by the independent Biodiversity Council on Tuesday describes Victoria as the “nature-poorest state”. It finds inadequate funding, weakened protections and inaction have left the state’s biodiversity in “serious decline”. Populations of Victoria’s threatened plants and animals were 70% smaller than they were in 2000, Melbourne residents had the worst access to green spaces of any Australian capital city and forests continued to be cleared – for fire breaks and via other loopholes – despite a commitment to end native forest logging in 2024. Meanwhile funding for biodiversity halved and Parks Victoria had a third fewer staff now than in 2020-21, the report says.

  • Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter

Prof Sarah Bekessey, a conservation scientist at the University of Melbourne and lead councillor at the Biodiversity Council, says the state is facing an “extinction emergency”, with a real risk that species could be lost in the next term of government. She says the critically endangered Victorian grassland earless dragon was “one that jumps to mind immediately”, given the state government’s failure to protect its last wild population.

“Victorians deeply, deeply care about nature,” Bekessey says, with surveys consistently showing the vast majority supported more action to protect the environment.

A Labor spokesperson says the government had “delivered real action to protect our environment so future generations can enjoy the best national parks in the world”. Its environment announcements in the campaign include support for a few local parks and $900,000 for Wildlife Victoria’s travelling vet service.

Jess Wilson’s Coalition has pledged $50m to establish a coastal environment resilience fund to tackle erosion and strengthen infrastructure, and to increase the number of park rangers. But the Coalition’s proposal to recover timber and fibre from 5,000 hectares of public forests through “targeted thinning” and fuel reduction each year has been widely criticised by the environment movement as native forest logging under the guise of fire management.

But the Coalition refutes that characterisation. “We aren’t bringing back native timber logging,” a spokesperson says. “The forest will come first. But if trees need to come down to reduce bushfire risk or for the health of the forest, then it makes sense to put that to its highest value, and in many cases that will be timber processing.”

Nationals MP Melina Bath told the Weekly Times the policy would deliver 100,000 to 200,000 tonnes of timber annually.

“That’s just logging,” says Lindenmayer. “It’s bullshit to say it’s about fire management. We know quite clearly that the way forests are thinned makes them more vulnerable to fire. And thinning actually takes out the habitat for animals like Leadbeater’s possum, which depends on the understory.”

“Victorians chose to leave native forest logging behind,” says Chris Schuringa, the nature campaigns coordinator at Environment Victoria. “The state government has spent more than $1bn transitioning the industry. Jess Wilson is living in a fantasy land if she thinks she can bring back native forest logging. It doesn’t make economic sense, it’s a disaster for the environment and has very, very low public support from Victorians.”

Schuringa says the Greens were the only party with a positive vision to protect forests, end all timber extraction apart from plantations, and close logging loopholes. During Tuesday’s leaders debate, the Greens leader, Ellen Sandell, said it was a “deep, deep shame” that the environment had been largely forgotten in the election. “We have a responsibility as governments and as politicians to be stewards of our environment for our kids and grandkids.”

Kos Samaras, director at polling group Redbridge, says most people still care about the environment, but it drops down the list of priorities at times of economic stress – “which we are seeing and experiencing right now”. However, Samaras says the environment remained a “very important” issue for younger voters, which could be a problem for Labor, given “the lack of policy in this space”.

Ipsos polling on the top issues facing Victoria shows voter concern for the environment peaked in 2020 – in the wake of the black summer bushfires – but is now at the lowest level in 15 years, a trend also reflected nationally.

A recent report commissioned by the Wilderness Society finds Victoria’s forests are worth more standing than cut down. The analysis finds nearly a third of the state’s economy, $210bn, depends on the natural environment: healthy forests supply water, parks drive regional tourism, coastal systems sustain fishers and trees shield towns from floods and keep neighbourhoods cool in a heatwave.

“The next Victorian government has an opportunity to halt the destruction of nature and start rebuilding, but it will take more than promises. We need proper funding, stronger laws and accountability for delivering results,” Bekessey says.

Lindenmayer says expanding parks and protected areas, such as the proposed Great Forest national park 90 minutes from Melbourne, could be a boon for both city residents and regional tourism. “It’s what the people of Melbourne want and need, we know that it will be good for the economy, and we know that it’ll be good for other elements of biodiversity that have declined dramatically.”

“It’s hard to deal with a constant diet of bad news,” he says. “What actually needs to happen is there needs to be some environmental wins, to give people hope.”

australia.title: ‘All civilians suck’: inside the disturbing world of ‘cop influencers’
australia.snippet: A new social media trend glorifies police and defence brutality. Many of the accounts are operated by current or former serving members G...
australia.content:
The footage is grainy, taken from a mobile phone across four lanes of a Melbourne freeway, but it is clear what it shows: heavily armed police in tactical clothing forcefully arresting a group of people near a four-wheel drive.

Six teenagers and young men involved in an alleged burglary and pursuit in a stolen car were arrested during the operation in October.

When a 16-year-old faced court the following day, his mother accused the police of violence.

“It was brutal,” she reportedly told the court. “The gun was smashed on his head. They used canines on him. It was extreme force.” The magistrate told her it was not the court’s role to question the police’s use of force. The arrest has been referred for independent investigation with oversight from professional standards officers.

But on Instagram, among a growing network of police and defence influencer accounts, the arrest was being spoken about in another way.

“FAFO [fuck around and find out] Melbourne edition,” one account posted.

“Sudanese B’Ballers get bounced,” wrote a former New South Wales police officer on another.

Both accounts have tens of thousands of followers and routinely show police at work, either undergoing operations such as that on the Monash Freeway, or more candid moments in stations or on patrol.

There are many other similar accounts, and many of them repost one another’s content, increasing the prominence of what have been dubbed pol- or cop-influencers.

The comments on these posts are often racist, sexist or condone police using any force necessary to carry out their duties.

Many are operated by current or former serving members, and exist as a subgenre within a larger ecosystem of defence and combat operations pages that promote personal and combat training businesses, tactical gear, stickers and collectible coins.

Rian Terrell, the police accountability practice lead at the Redfern Legal Centre, said if current NSW police officers were involved in posting material on the pages they could be breaching code of conduct guidelines.

“Social media content that valorises using excessive force and mocks compliance with the law is wholly inconsistent with the solemn legal responsibility that police officers have to obey the law and only use force that is reasonably necessary,” he said.

“This cultural problem may flow down into daily decisions by police officers to use excessive force and to flout legal requirements.”

Several inquiries have identified cultural problems within defence and police forces, including one that found the SAS operated like a “bikie gang” with an “uncontrolled warrior ethos”. The racism and “paramilitarisation” within police forces was also considered during the Kumanjayi Walker inquest.

The accounts appear to include a mix of content aggregated from elsewhere including official media and police social media accounts, images and footage provided to them by current or former serving members, or taken themselves.

The accounts also promote podcasts or events where former police or defence members have appeared.

In some cases, the accounts fundraise for causes including that of the NSW police officer Benedict Bryant, who was found guilty last year of dangerous driving occasioning death after he placed his unmarked police vehicle in the path of a stolen trail bike ridden by Indigenous teenager Jai Wright.

An account that has recently received prominence within the network of pol-influencer accounts is Epic 1 Two, the label launched by the former SAS soldier Ben Roberts-Smith, who is facing charges of murdering or ordering the murders of five unarmed detainees while deployed in Afghanistan between 2009 and 2012. Roberts-Smith denies the allegations.

The label’s Instagram account has more than 100,000 followers, and has been boosted by several prominent defence-related influencer accounts.

Among those to have promoted Roberts-Smith’s new label are the convicted US war criminal Eddie Gallagher, who posted a video of himself wearing an Epic 1 Two hoodie.

“Like me, Australian SAS veteran and Victoria Cross recipient Ben Roberts-Smith has faced serious allegations stemming from his time in combat, along with intense media scrutiny and a legal battle that impacts far more than just the individual,” Gallagher wrote in the post.

‘Exceptionalism and masculinity’

Prof Ben Wadham, the director of a Flinders University initiative to improve the wellbeing of veterans and their families, said defence-related Instagram accounts were an evolution of a practice which started decades earlier, when veterans shared hard copies of photographs taken on duty with their colleagues.

But Wadham, a former Australian Army corporal who served in the infantry, said there was a “dangerous aspect” to the shift of this environment online.

“It’s a bunch of people talking to themselves, and they tend to be pretty prejudiced, extreme in their language and thinking and statements, about women, about anything that’s different,” he said.

“It’s almost promoting an infantry caliphate: all civilians suck, every one else sucks, no one understands us … all the posts are about reinforcing their exceptionalism.

“The sexualisation and racial and prejudicial stuff all serve the same function: reinforcing that we’re a brotherhood, we’re doing something unique … [it’s about] exceptionalism and masculinity.”

Wadham said that a likely justification for some of the posts would be that they were “dark humour” that civilians wouldn’t understand because they had not served.

He also said the accounts existed within a broader “rightwing, martial, soldier-y” context, which involved podcasters like Joe Rogan and promoted “the idea that the world is dangerous and we walk the halls so the world can sleep safely at night”.

Guardian Australia asked the defence department, as well as police forces in Victoria, NSW and Queensland, whether the content posted on specific accounts breached internal guidelines. We also asked how many breaches of the guidelines had been recorded.

Defence declined to comment. But defence personnel are required to comply with policies governing the appropriate use of personal social media, including protecting sensitive and private information, maintaining professional standards, and upholding defence values.

These obligations apply regardless of whether content is shared under a real name, pseudonym or anonymously.

Victoria police was the only force to confirm how many breaches of social media policy it had investigated: 16 between 1 October last year and 30 September this year, with one matter resulting in a disciplinary charge.

The case was not heard as the employee resigned, police said. Such breaches can be handled by local officers, Professional Standards Command, or the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission.

“Victoria Police employees are expected to use social media responsibly and conduct themselves in accordance with Victoria Police values and professional standards at all times,” police said in a statement.

“Current and former members are also bound by sections … of the Victoria Police Act, which relate to disclosure of police information.

“Employees must not disclose unauthorised information or post content that is offensive, discriminatory, defamatory, threatening, bullying or otherwise inappropriate.”

Victoria police would not comment on two posts provided by the Guardian of former officers sharing details about their work on Instagram, which included images of tactical operations.

Queensland police would not comment on posts that show a serving member identifying themselves and sharing information about their work.

NSW police did not respond to a request for comment.

Within a week of posting about the Monash Freeway arrest, one of the prominent Instagram accounts monitored by the Guardian had moved on to something else: promoting Make Diggers Violent Again clothing with a video featuring a Queensland shooting range.

“If violence isn’t the answer,” one person posted in the comments, “then you’re asking the wrong questions.”

australia.title: Australia urged to wean off imported fossil fuels amid global supply shocks
australia.snippet: Grattan Institute report calls on government to ‘seize’ opportunity to cap diesel tax credits, introduce EV subsidies for less wealthy’ a...
australia.content:
Capping lucrative diesel tax handouts to big business, building new “clean” refineries and targeting electric vehicle subsidies to less wealthy people could save Australians thousands of dollars in fuel per year, according to a major new report calling on the government to reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels.

The Grattan Institute, one of the nation’s most respected thinktanks, has warned Australia imports too much of its fuel, and that the country must brace for more global supply shocks – like that from the war in Iran. Under a plan already attracting criticism from business groups, Grattan urged diesel handouts to mining and primary industries be curbed in favour of incentives for electric trucks and a huge expansion of the EV charging network.

“Relying on fuel imports during an era of benign international relations and dependable strategic partners was a passable strategy. But in a more dangerous and unpredictable world, it is no longer tenable,” the report, released on Sunday, warned.

“Australia should expect the coming decades to be less stable than the past one. This means bracing, and preparing, for more oil shocks.”

Australia imports 97% of its liquid fuel. Grattan’s fuel plan report, Fuelling the Future, warns this “leaves us dangerously exposed to supply disruptions and price hikes”.

It argues that the US-Israel war in Iran has driven up inflation and cost Australians nearly $18bn, and the federal government directly at least $3bn, creating an opportunity the government “should seize” to boost fuel security.

Very little liquid fuel is produced or refined in Australia, with only two domestic oil refineries. But rather than boosting that number, Grattan says Australia should lower its reliance on imported fuels and fossil fuels generally by shifting towards EVs, including an ambitious target of 650,000 electric trucks nationwide by 2050.

That alone would cut Australia’s diesel use by 5bn litres a year, Grattan forecast. The report also calls for the fuel tax credit program – which costs Australia billions each year – to be capped at $35m per corporate group annually.

The biggest user of that program – which refunds taxes on fuel for machinery and heavy vehicles travelling on private, rather than public, roads – is the mining sector. The fuel tax credit scheme has become a political hot-button issue, with big business campaigning for it to be preserved amid calls for it to be reined in.

Tania Constable, CEO of the Minerals Council of Australia, rejected the Grattan proposal.

“Australia does need stronger fuel security, but making diesel more expensive for regional industries won’t create a single extra litre of fuel, build a refinery or improve supply-chain resilience. Instead, it would increase costs for miners, farmers, freight operators and regional businesses, with those costs ultimately flowing through to Australian households,” she said.

“If the goal is greater energy security, then Australia should be focused on increasing domestic production, expanding refining capacity and building more resilient supply chains – not making essential fuel more expensive.”

But the Grattan report says capping the scheme would save the government $3bn annually, and hasten the electrification of the mining sector – which it said would help the mining sector in the long run.

The report also recommends the government invest $1.1bn in a national network of chargers for EVs, as well as provide $2.4bn in vouchers for trucking firms to buy electric trucks. It calls for federal vehicle standards to be boosted to incentivise cleaner cars, as well as a restructuring of EV subsidies “to target people least able to afford them”.

Labor is widely expected to restrict current EV subsidies in next month’s mid-year economic update, as the government searches for budget savings.

In other areas of fuel use, Grattan notes Australia produces no “clean” jet fuel, and recommends the government direct $6bn to the first generation of so-called “clean refineries” to make that fuel.

Grattan says these refineries could provide nearly 10bn litres of clean jet fuel per year by 2050, but notes that it could cost $100bn to build them all, and that importing clean jet fuel would be cheaper.

But it argues that $6bn – the savings generated from just two years of capping the fuel tax credits to mining companies – would cover a quarter of the cost of the first five refineries, kickstarting the sector and providing fuel security in future supply shocks.

“Historically, making fuel meant making fossil fuels. But in an age of electrification and clean fuels, Australia now has more options,” the report said.

world.title: California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
world.snippet: Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded Multiple coastal hazard warnings we...
world.content:
Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.

Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

Nearly 72,000 people have been evacuated from areas of Odisha in eastern India as Tropical Cyclone Akvan approaches land. Akvan is expected to make landfall on Friday between Narsapur and Puri, prompting cyclone warnings from the India Meteorological Department for north Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and south Odisha coasts. Peak wind gusts are expected to reach 70mph, with rainfall totals through Friday and Saturday potentially exceeding 200mm for northern coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.

After a yellow level 2 severe thunderstorm warning by the South African Weather Service on Tuesday, torrential rainfall and large hail were reported across parts of Johannesburg. The storms triggered flash flooding and caused infrastructure damage in the township of Soweto. One person died, while another remains missing after the severe storms.

world.title: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked
world.snippet: The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits Environmentalists in South Afri...
world.content:
Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.

The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.

The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.

The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.

The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.

Otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, said: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.”

Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, said she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted quickly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them.

“As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their new leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she said.

The rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres.

Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them.

“A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” said Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.”

Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit.

The trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.”

Baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants.

The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” said Venter.

A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping company allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.

Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

world.title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
world.snippet: Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds One in four women around ...
world.content:
One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.

In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.

Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.

“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”

The Maputo protocol, a landmark treaty adopted by the African Union in 2003, guarantees women’s rights and obliges states to protect women from violence. It affirms that marriage must be based on full consent and guarantees women’s right to health.

“The underlying principle is unambiguous: sexual intercourse without free and voluntary consent constitutes sexual violence, including within marriage,” said Murunga. “Marriage does not create perpetual or implied consent. A woman retains the right to decide whether, when and how she engages in sexual activity”.

He said that as a first step rape laws across the continent needed to change. According to Murunga’s 2024 report, rape within marriage is not criminalised in some African countries. Seven countries expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Some countries, such as Tanzania and Eritrea, only criminalise marital rape when the couple do not live together.

In countries where child marriage is permitted and marital rape is not criminalised, children are left unprotected. A legal loophole is created for what, outside marriage, would be classed as rape, and young wives have few options when it comes to protecting themselves from sexual violence and exploitation. In Gabon, for example, when a man has married a child he abducted, he can only be prosecuted after the marriage is annulled.

Underpinning these laws is the mistaken belief that marital rape does not exist as a concept because, by marrying, wives are assumed to have permanently consented to sex with their husbands. In many areas, religion plays a key role in affirming these beliefs.

Alimatu Dimonekene, founder of A Girl At A Time, an organisation supporting adolescent girls in Sierra Leone, said a conversation around consent in marriage had yet to begin in Africa. “We’ve not even started the conversation [around marital rape],” she said. “Women will never call it rape; they make excuses for it or even blame themselves.”

She added: “In west Africa, sex is seen as an obligation in marriage. You must do whatever your husband demands.

“Once he has paid your bride price [a traditional marriage custom in which the bride’s family are paid money, livestock or goods by the groom], he owns you and you cannot reject his demands. Whatever he wants, he gets, including in terms of intimacy, finances and raising the children.”

world.title: Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling
world.snippet: A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza Fears are growing that the US could impose ...
world.content:
Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.

It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.

The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.

The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.

Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.

The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.

The US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also announced sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.

The Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize. She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.

Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.

Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians.”

In remarks addressed to Pillay, he said: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”

In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”

He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.

Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.

In the Myanmar case, a 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states, argued that the ICJ, in judging intent to commit genocide, should examine a range of “facts and circumstances” assessed “comprehensively and holistically”.

It also stressed that genocide was not solely defined by killings, and that the treatment of children, gender-based violence and forced displacement were also relevant.

The US until recently had taken a relatively more benign view of The Hague-based ICJ, and under Antony Blinken as US secretary of state determined that Myanmar had committed genocide.

The 15 ICJ judges are elected for nine-year terms by the UN security council and the UN general assembly.

Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before he imposes sanctions.

On Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan. The shelving of the near-dormant inquiry came after it was agreed evidence would be hard to obtain, but one side-effect may be a greater willingness on the part of the US to abandon its plan to impose sanctions on the ICC.

world.title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
world.snippet: Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans The European Commission has been a...
world.content:
The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.

The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.

The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists, the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor, Lina Attalah.

Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news”, for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.

The spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. While the EU conditions on democracy and rights are vague, the loans impose much more specific requirements on Egypt to carry out economic reforms.

Separate data sources – from leaked EU documents and deleted from an Egyptian government website – raise questions about the European Commission’s claims that Egypt met targets linked to social welfare programmes, which enabled the EU to release €2.5bn in assistance.

In confidential documents, the commission told EU lawmakers that Egypt had “broadly fulfilled” and then “fulfilled” two separate targets to increase the numbers of poor people on social welfare programmes between 2024 and 2026. But data points to a net reduction of 85,734 households as the Egyptian government removed people from its welfare programmes rather than expanded coverage.

If Egypt had expanded the programmes in line with the EU’s apparent conditions – and not removed any households – about 245,000 households, equivalent to roughly 909,000 people, would be getting these benefits. (The Guardian used World Bank data to make this rough calculation).

According to the leaked documents, the commission wanted Egypt to “further expand cash transfer programmes”, but despite a net reduction in beneficiaries it gave the green light anyway to two separate “soft” loans totalling €2.5bn.

In response to the Guardian’s findings, one of the European parliament’s leading spokespeople on EU-Egypt relations, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, said she was introducing a question to the European Commission demanding clarification.

“The finding by this investigation that the commission is seemingly sugarcoating Egypt’s performance is worrying,” Strik said. “From the beginning, the commission has used macro-financial assistance primarily as a tool to lure Egypt into migration cooperation, while considering formal conditions and its reporting obligations towards parliament as an inconvenient formality.”

Under the plan, Egypt has so far received €3.5bn in soft loans in three instalments, with a final payment of €1.5bn expected before the end of 2027.

The charge of sugarcoating figures relates to two social welfare programmes: the Takaful and Karama cash transfer programmes for poor and vulnerable households.

The Takaful (Solidarity) programme gives poor families cash payments as long as recipients have regular health visits and good attendance at school. The Karama (Dignity) programme gives unconditional cash payments to people living with a disability, older people, orphans and widows.

One of the EU conditions for Egypt to gain the first €1bn loan was to increase the number of Takaful and Karama beneficiary households by 100,000 to 4.7 million.

In a leaked report to lawmakers in the EU council of ministers and the European parliament, the commission described that requirement as “broadly fulfilled”.

The data in that report, however, reveals a net fall of 62,281 households during this period, owing to what the EU officials describe as “a multi-annual recertification process”. Some beneficiaries were added to the list but a larger number were removed because they were deemed ineligible.

In order to achieve a later instalment of €1.5bn, Egypt was required to “further expand” the programmes, adding 60,000 households to the Takaful and Karama beneficiaries list. A second leaked report to EU lawmakers shows that the commission concluded the target was “fulfilled” because 442,118 families were added to the list.

On this occasion, the commission did not report on numbers removed. Figures from Egypt’s ministry of social solidarity, however, show a net reduction of 23,453 beneficiaries to the programmes in the 11 months until June 2026, the period leading up to the release of that payment. The EU announced the release of the €1.5bn payment in July 2026.

The data has since been deleted from the Egyptian ministry website but the Guardian has seen screenshots and archived webpages.

During a period from 2024 to 26 when the EU required Egypt to add 160,000 households to the rolls of the Karama and Takaful programmes, there was a net decline of 85,734 households.

Timothy Kaldas, the deputy director of the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, said the commission had generally “done a poor job of leveraging the funds of European taxpayers to support genuine stabilisation” on the other side of the Mediterranean. “The strategic interest of Europe is seeing a more economically stable Egypt with a population that is less precarious,” he said.

Sandra Gómez López, a Spanish socialist MEP who recently visited Cairo to assess human rights in Egypt, said the data presented by the Guardian raised important questions. “The commission must explain transparently why it considers these commitments to have been fulfilled and demonstrate that European funding is genuinely contributing to improving social protection for the Egyptian population,” she said.

She stressed that the EU should not withdraw support, “but neither can we allow the country’s strategic importance to lead us to lower our standards when it comes to human rights”.

For critics, the questions about the EU’s willingness to hold Egypt accountable on very precise socioeconomic targets do not bode well for the broader but less defined goals for democracy and human rights.

Strik said: “The fact that Egypt and the commission even seem to ignore the crystal-clear socioeconomic conditions doesn’t increase my expectation that they adhere to the vague precondition on democracy and the rule of law.”

Claudio Francavilla, an associate EU director at Human Rights Watch, said: “Without benchmarks, the EU has turned a human rights conditionality into a blank cheque for Egypt’s authoritarianism.”

In a statement to the Guardian, the European Commission said the policy target on Takaful and Karama referred to new beneficiary families “and not to its net increase”. The spokesperson said there was “no contradiction” between this statement and that in a confidential document that said Egypt was required to “further expand cash transfer programmes”.

Asked about the release of the remaining €1.5bn in promised loans, the commission said it “will be made once all conditions have been met”, referring to 24 economic policy conditions, keeping an IMF programme on track and “taking concrete and credible steps towards respecting effective democratic mechanisms, including a multiparty parliamentary system, and the rule of law, and guaranteeing respect for human rights”.

It added: “Compliance with the conditionality is examined thoroughly” by EU officials and diplomats based on “information provided by the Egyptian authorities and other relevant sources”.

Egypt’s mission to the EU in Brussels did not respond to a request for comment.
